newsitem.title: PERU: Peru captives set for Easter under rebel guns.
newsitem.headline: Peru captives set for Easter under rebel guns.

text.p: Hostages held by Marxist rebels in the besieged Japanese ambassador's home looked certain on Wednesday to spend Easter in captivity even as speculation mounted in Peru about a possible deal to end the crisis.
The 72 male hostages have already spent Christmas and New Year away from their families during 14 agonizing weeks under the gun of 20-odd heavily-armed Tupac Amaru rebels.
But despite the rumours of an imminent asylum agreement swirling round diplomatic and media circles in Lima, no one seriously expected them out for Easter weekend celebrations.

Diplomats said both the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were close to agreement on an asylum deal, but other elements of a negotiated solution were still being hotly debated.
Peruvians, whose Christmas festivities were overshadowed by the hostage crisis which began on Dec. 17, were again preparing to focus their religious holiday on the captives.
The Roman Catholic bishop of Lima's neighbouring port Callao, Miguel Irizar, said a Via Crucis (Way of the Cross) procession would be held on Friday in honour of the captives.
"Let's hope that Easter ends with the freedom of all the hostages, because in a certain way, we also feel like prisoners in the Japanese ambassador's residence," he said.
Others planned special masses and candlelit vigils around the country to show solidarity with the hostages.
Local media were speculating that a behind-the-scenes deal, masterminded by a three-man guarantors' commission overseeing negotiations to end the 99-day crisis, was taking shape.

The daily La Republica said on Wednesday the deal, to be finalised next week, included the freedom of some low-ranking MRTA prisoners, an amnesty and ransom payment to the rebels, and asylum in Cuba or the Dominican Republic for the hostage-takers.
The MRTA has from the outset demanded the freedom of all its roughly 450 prisoners in Peru, while President Alberto Fujimori's government has consistently ruled this out.
There was speculation, however, that some releases might be allowed under a special commission set up before the crisis to award pardons to prisoners falsely accused of terrorism.
The MRTA and government negotiators have not met directly since March 12, but were expected to sit down again on Monday in a safe house opposite the residence used for talks.
Neither the MRTA nor Fujimori have commented on the specifics of negotiations, although both have blamed the other for the standoff while expressing a willingness to negotiate a peaceful solution.

Fuelling the speculation on Wednesday, a guarantors' sub- commission charged with checking jail conditions for MRTA members was due to visit the high-altitude Yanamayo jail in the Andean region of Puno.

Lori Berenson, a U.S. citizen, is serving a life sentence at Yanamayo after her treason conviction for allegedly helping the MRTA plot a takeover of Congress. Also held there is an MRTA leader, Miguel Rincon, and Nancy Gilbonio, girlfriend of Nestor Cerpa, commander of the MRTA rebels holding the Japanese residence.
Continuing a traditional practice, Peru granted Easter pardons on Wednesday to 91 prisoners, but their sentences were unrelated to crimes committed by any of the country's two leftist rebel groups.
